transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-14
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jared Collins (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Velez (Redwood SE), Aisha Wyatt (CSM) --- Lina Park (QuasarMetrics Head of ML), Ethan Zhou (Platform), Priya Nair (SRE), Marco Reyes (Product)

---
Summary:
QuasarMetrics is scoping a 4-6 week POC to validate Redwood's hosted vs dedicated cost/latency tradeoffs for their real-time insights product. Primary goals: size capacity for their bursty usage (nominal QPS 80-120, peak bursts to 2k QPS sustained for 30s-2min), evaluate tail latency at p99/p999 for 256/512 token outputs, and validate workload replay and benchmark methodology. Customer emphasized data residency and audit logs (SOC2 + SSO), and wants a playbook for tail mitigation (prefetch, prefix caching, dynamic batching).

Topics covered:
- Workload trajectory (steady-state vs ramp vs flash-burst)
- Token distribution (input prompt len, output len, avg vs 95th pct)
- Concurrency model and kv/prefix cache behavior
- Benchmark design (replay, synthetic gaussian vs heavy-tail)
- Success criteria and timelines

Action items (recap in call): see metadata above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jared (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the quota and the burst shapes you sent.
[00:12] Lina (QuasarMetrics): Hi hi, Lina here. Thanks, Jared. Sorry we're a little late, had a deploy.
[00:17] Ethan (QuasarMetrics): Ethan on my side.
[00:19] Priya (QuasarMetrics): Priya, SRE.
[00:21] Marco (QuasarMetrics): Marco, product.
[00:23] Maya (Redwood SE): Maya, Redwood SE. I'll drive the replay and benchmark talk.
[00:27] Carlos (Redwood): Carlos, solutions eng, I'll cover quantization/kerneled perf notes.

[00:35] Jared: Okay first high level — Lina, can you give us the traffic profile you expect day one and then six months? I want QPS, concurrency, and token shape if you have it.
[00:44] Lina: Yes so day one we're targeting low double-digit QPS, like 80 to 120 qps average during business hours, bursty. But the product is event-driven; during certain campaigns we see flash bursts — we've seen up to two thousand qps for short windows, about 30 seconds to two minutes. The content is relatively short prompts: user message about 60 tokens on average, output target around 180 to 320 tokens usually but 95th pct is near 512. There's also a few long-form reports that generate 1k+ tokens but those are rare, maybe 0.3% of requests.
[01:25] Maya: Cool, that's helpful. When you say bursts to 2k QPS, is that uniformly distributed across users or concentrated?
[01:31] Lina: concentrated — a small set of accounts trigger, so concurrency per model instance can be skewed. So we care about tail and hot-keying.
[01:38] Priya: Also to add our SLA ask: P99 should be under 250ms for 64-token outputs and p99 for 256 tokens under 700ms ideally. For 512 tokens we expect p99 to be under 1.2s but that's negotiable depending on dedicated vs hosted. p999 is a concern — we want 99.9 to be predictable within a factor, not spiky.
[02:00] Carlos: Quick note, p999 depends a lot on KV cache pressure and batch sizing — if you have lots of long outputs that evict the cache you'll see tail blow up.
[02:10] Ethan: What's Redwood's typical strategy to mitigate that? We can't change user behavior.
[02:13] Maya: Two levers — prefix/KV caching for repeated conversation prefixes and adaptive batching with a burst window. For hot accounts we can route to dedicated pools or use a warm-warm path where we keep KV pinned. We call it warmpin in the playbook (may be typed differently in docs).
[02:35] Lina: Warmpin, ok. Another dimension is token mix: our input tokens are often short, but output tokens dominate cost and latency. We want to understand the cost delta if we drop to a 16-bit quant or use int8-ff or q4_0.
[02:47] Carlos: Right — quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput but can affect accuracy. For throughput sizing we usually benchmark 256 and 512 output profiles across q8/q4 variants and measure p50/p95/p99/p999 and tail.
[03:03] Marco: On security — we need SOC2, SSO with SAML, audit logs, and KMS for encryption. Also data residency — we need EU-hosted logs for some clients.
[03:14] Jared: All standard — we'll attach the compliance pack. For Private deployments we can do VPC peering and HSM/KMS integration; for hosted we have regional tenancy.

[03:28] Maya: Ok diving into benchmark design. We're proposing a 72-hour replay plus targeted synthetic bursts. Step one: you provide a 72-hour ingress trace with per-request metadata (timestamp, user id hashed, prompt length, expected output length distribution). Step two: we convert to a replay script that supports compressed record rate ramps and preserves inter-arrival times, including the flash-burst windows. We'll run on Redwood Dedicated preview cluster with both hosted and dedicated routing to compare.
[04:05] Ethan: Can replay simulate backpressure from downstream? Sometimes our infra retries and that amplifies load.
[04:10] Maya: We can inject retry patterns and client-side backoff scenarios. Addendum: please include any retry multipliers in the trace.
[04:18] Lina: We'll add that. What's the typical concurrency mapping? If we see 2k QPS for 60s, what's the concurrency per model shard?
[04:26] Carlos: That depends on latencies. Rough math: concurrency = QPS * latency. If you have 0.6s average latency for 256 tokens, 2k QPS -> 1.2k concurrent requests. Shard sizing: a single A100-like pool can handle X tokens depending on quant and batch. We have a sizing playbook — we'll run model-specific microbenchmarks.
[04:47] Priya: We also want to validate cost at different tail SLOs. Can you output per-token cost and per-request cost in the benchmark results?
[04:53] Maya: Yes — we'll provide token-level cost breakdown (encoding + decode + KV cache cost amortized) and an end-to-end cost curve across request sizes.
[05:00] Jared: Let's capture success criteria now — Lina?
[05:04] Lina: OK success criteria: 1) For our interactive baseline (64–256 tokens) p99 must be <=750ms on dedicated; hosted must be within 20% of that during non-peak. 2) During flash bursts to 2k QPS, tail p999 degradation should be bounded such that 95% of spikes remain within 2x baseline; and we need a documented mitigation route (route to dedicated, degrade to condensed output, or async enqueue). 3) Replayed benchmarks accurately represent cost within 15% of production observed cost. 4) Security checklist passed for SOC2 items listed.
[05:39] Carlos: I'll add that we should measure cold-start penalties (model swap time) if you plan to scale down between bursts — that is often a hidden tail cost.
[05:48] Marco: For timelines — are you thinking 4 weeks or 6 weeks POC? We need a playbook we can run quickly.
[05:54] Jared: We usually do a 4-6 week run: week 0 onboarding + trace handoff, week 1 replay and initial microbenchmarks, week 2 targeted bursts and model variant testing (quant, batch), week 3 results analysis and playbook handoff. If security review also happens it'll push to 6 weeks.
[06:12] Priya: Who will run the replay? Our infra or Redwood?
[06:16] Maya: We can run it in collaboration. We typically run first replay to ensure experiment integrity, then hand you the container to run in your environment if you prefer.
[06:25] Ethan: About model variants — can you show us results for both a 7B and a 13B-ish open model? We want to know cost and latency delta.
[06:32] Carlos: Yes — we'll include a 7B and 13B quant matrix. Also a 30B-ish proxy for longform checks if you want. We'll include kernel-opt runs vs naive to show gains.
[06:42] Lina: Are there any caveats with tokenization differences across models that will skew the replay?
[06:46] Maya: Tokenization differences matter. For fairness we normalize by tokenized length under each model and include raw char-length in the trace so we can map. We'll show both tokens-per-request and chars-per-request metrics.
[06:59] Marco: For the flash-burst mitigation — can you run an experiment where you route top 5% keys to a hot pool with pinned KV and compare p999?
[07:06] Maya: Yes we call that hot-key pinning and we'll run it. It's part of the playbook.
[07:12] Ethan: What's your expected run cadence for the benchmark? One big run across 72 hours or multiple short runs?
[07:18] Carlos: We'll do a 72-hour continuous replay to capture diurnal and microburst patterns and then run synthetic targeted bursts (e.g., 2k QPS for 60s, 5x longer tail bursts) to isolate tail effects.
[07:31] Priya: On observability we want per-request trace ids, token counts, model id, quant profile, and an SLO dashboard export. Is that available?
[07:39] Aisha (CSM): Yes, Redwood Console will provide per-route dashboards and we can add a custom export with traces and token breakdowns. We'll add an integration note for your observability tools.
[07:51] Lina: A few odd questions — do you support customer-side rate limiting or can you do server-side graceful degradation?
[07:59] Jared: Both. You can implement per-customer quotas client-side, and we provide server-side routing policies: fallback to smaller model, fall back to cached response, or queue with async callback.
[08:12] Marco: How do you handle retries? We don't want retry storms to double the load.
[08:16] Maya: We add idempotency tokens and server-side dedupe for short windows; replay scripts can simulate retry storms if needed.
[08:24] Lina: For the security bit, we'll need an architecture review — can you send an on-call contact?
[08:29] Jared: I'll include an infra contact and a security lead; we'll attach the SOC2 and compliance packet.
[08:34] Marco: On cost: can you produce a curve: cost per 1k requests for 64/256/512 token outputs across hosted vs dedicated?
[08:41] Carlos: Yes we'll run per-token cost accounting and produce a cost curve with error bars.
[08:47] Priya: One more thing — we have a small subset of requests that are multimodal (image prompt + text) — is that in scope?
[08:55] Maya: We can include a small sample, but that complicates benchmarking because of different model classes. Recommend isolating multimodal traffic or running it as a separate track.
[09:06] Ethan: For the replay artifact — do you have a preferred format? We use gzipped newline-delimited json with fields: ts, user_hash, prompt, expected_tokens, retry_count.
[09:16] Maya: That's perfect. Add tokenized_length per model if you can or we can compute it during preprocessing.
[09:22] Lina: We'll prepare that and include example snippet.
[09:26] Jared: Great. Next steps recap — we need the trace by Monday, we'll stand up the replay, run microbenchmarks, and reconvene for results. Any blockers?
[09:36] Marco: No blockers, security will review the compliance pack; Priya will coordinate.
[09:41] Priya: Yup.
[09:43] Carlos: One final note: cold restart time for model swap varies a lot across quant and instance types — we'll measure that as part of the replay and include it in the playbook as a hidden tail cost.
[09:55] Lina: Helpful. Thanks all.
[09:58] Jared: Alright thanks everyone, we'll send the benchmark plan and schedule the replay run.
[10:03] Maya: I'll follow up with the runbook and container link.
[10:06] Aisha: I'll attach the compliance docs and a pricing worksheet.
[10:09] Meeting end.
